items.short: How far the balance wheel swings in degrees. A healthy movement typically shows about 270–310° when fully wound.
Hand-bevelling and polishing the edges of movement parts at 45°, a hallmark of fine finishing.
A calendar complication that adjusts for 30- and 31-day months automatically and needs correcting only once a year, at the end of February.
An hour marker made as a separate piece and fixed onto the dial, rather than printed.
A mechanical movement that winds itself using a rotor that spins as your wrist moves.
The oscillating wheel that, with the hairspring, divides time into equal beats. The heart of a mechanical watch.
How many times the balance swings per hour, in vibrations per hour (vph). 28,800 vph is 8 beats per second, or 4 Hz.
The ring around the crystal. It can be fixed, or rotate to measure elapsed time, a second time zone or speed.
A metal band made of links, as opposed to a strap.
The name or number of a specific movement design, for example ETA 2824-2. Also spelled caliber.
Rolex's name for its scratch- and fade-resistant ceramic bezel inserts.
A very hard, scratch-resistant material (usually zirconium oxide) used for bezels and cases.
A watch with a built-in stopwatch, usually operated by two pushers beside the crown.
A watch whose movement has passed an official accuracy test, such as COSC (−4/+6 s/day for mechanical movements).
An escapement invented by George Daniels that reduces sliding friction, so it needs less lubrication. Industrialised by Omega in 1999.
A castellated wheel that coordinates the start, stop and reset of a chronograph. Prized for its smooth pusher feel.
Any function beyond showing hours, minutes and seconds, such as a date, chronograph or moon phase.
A mechanism that delivers the same energy to the escapement regardless of how wound the mainspring is.
Contrôle Officiel Suisse des Chronomètres, the Swiss body that tests and certifies chronometer movements.
"Geneva stripes": parallel decorative waves applied to movement plates and rotors.
The knob on the side of the case used to wind the watch and set the time and date.
The transparent cover over the dial: acrylic (hesalite), mineral glass or sapphire.
An opening in the dial that shows the date disc underneath.
Faceted, tapering hands shaped like an elongated triangle, classic on dress watches.
A chronometer escapement historically used in marine chronometers. Very accurate, but sensitive to shocks.
The face of the watch, carrying markers, hands and text.
A unidirectional rotating bezel with a 60-minute scale, used to track elapsed dive time. It only turns one way so an accidental knock can only shorten the shown time.
A partly finished base movement supplied to a brand, which then finishes, decorates or modifies it.
Citizen's light-powered quartz technology. A solar cell under the dial charges a rechargeable cell.
The mechanism that releases the energy of the mainspring in tiny, regular steps. It makes the tick.
A sapphire caseback that lets you see the movement.
A chronograph that can be reset and restarted with a single press of the reset pusher while running.
A watch assembled from parts of different watches and passed off as original.
A cone-shaped pulley linked to the barrel by a chain. It evens out the mainspring's force as it unwinds.
Poinçon de Genève: a quality hallmark for movements made and finished in the Canton of Geneva to strict criteria.
A complication that shows a second time zone, usually with an extra 24-hour hand.
Enamel fired at very high temperatures in multiple layers. Produces dials of extraordinary depth and permanence.
New watches sold by dealers who are not authorised by the brand, often at a discount (or a premium).
Precise repeating patterns engraved into a dial with a rose engine or straight-line engine.
A feature that stops the seconds hand when you pull out the crown, so you can set the time to the second.
A very fine spiral spring attached to the balance wheel. Its elasticity sets the rhythm of the watch.
High-accuracy quartz: thermocompensated movements accurate to around ±10 seconds per year.
Omega's name for its acrylic crystal. It scratches easily, but the scratches polish out and it does not shatter.
A movement running at 36,000 vph (5 Hz) or faster, for better stability and finer chronograph resolution.
A watch that closely imitates a famous design under its own brand name. Legal, but debated.
A movement designed and made by the watch brand itself rather than bought from a supplier.
The international standard for dive watches, covering water resistance, legibility in the dark, shock resistance and more.
The international standard for anti-magnetic watches.
The ability of a balance to keep the same rate whether its swing (amplitude) is large or small.
A synthetic ruby used as a low-friction bearing for pivots in the movement. Jewel count is not a measure of quality on its own.
A display where the hour number jumps instantly to the next one instead of being shown with a hand.
The Swiss lever escapement: the near-universal escapement in mechanical wristwatches, descended from Thomas Mudge's 18th-century invention.
The distance from the top lug tip to the bottom lug tip. It matters more than diameter for how a watch fits your wrist.
The gap between the lugs where the strap fits, in millimetres. Tells you which straps will fit.
Luminous material on hands and markers that glows in the dark, usually Super-LumiNova or LumiBrite.
Exposure to magnets (speakers, phone cases, bag clasps) can make a mechanical watch run very fast. A watchmaker can demagnetise it in seconds.
The coiled spring in the barrel that stores the energy of a mechanical watch.
A mechanical movement you wind by turning the crown, with no rotor. Also called hand-wound.
A quartz movement with a mechanical chronograph module, giving a snappy pusher feel at low cost.
The Swiss Federal Institute of Metrology. It certifies Omega's Master Chronometers to 0/+5 s/day and 15,000 gauss resistance.
A small, often online-only watch brand, frequently founded by enthusiasts.
A chiming complication that sounds the hours, quarter-hours and minutes on demand using tiny hammers and gongs.
A display showing the current phase of the moon, usually through a disc in a dial aperture.
The engine of a watch: the mechanism that keeps and displays time.
A one-piece fabric strap that threads under the watch. Originally military, now a cheap way to change a watch's look.
A decorative pattern of overlapping small circles applied to movement plates.
A calendar that accounts for months of different lengths and leap years, correct until the year 2100.
How long a fully wound watch runs before stopping, typically 38–80 hours.
A movement regulated by a quartz crystal vibrating at 32,768 Hz. Far more accurate than mechanical and cheaper to make.
A split-seconds chronograph with two seconds hands, used to time two events that start together.
A dial that has been refinished or repainted. It dramatically reduces the value of a vintage watch.
A secondary spring rewound at regular intervals to deliver constant force to the escapement.
The weighted, pivoting semicircle in an automatic movement that winds the mainspring.
Synthetic sapphire crystal: very scratch-resistant, used on most quality watches.
A crown that screws onto a threaded tube to seal the case, important for water resistance.
A modern material for hairsprings and escapement parts. Anti-magnetic, light and needs no lubrication.
A watch whose movement and dial have been cut away to show the mechanism.
A chiming watch that strikes the hours (and quarters) automatically as they pass. Grande sonnerie strikes hours and quarters every quarter.
Seiko's hybrid technology: a mainspring drives the hands, while a quartz-controlled electromagnetic brake regulates them, giving a gliding seconds hand.
A central seconds hand that moves in small, rapid steps, appearing to sweep round the dial.
A scale on a chronograph bezel or dial used to calculate speed over a known distance.
An instrument that listens to a movement and measures its rate, amplitude and beat error.
A rotating cage carrying the escapement and balance, invented by Breguet in 1801 to average out errors caused by gravity.
A radioactive luminous material used on watches from the 1960s to late 1990s. It ages to a creamy patina.
A display where the hour numeral travels along an arc to indicate the minutes.
The pressure a watch is tested to, shown in metres or ATM. 30 m means splash-proof, 100 m is fine for swimming, and 200 m or more is a dive watch.
A complication that shows the time in all 24 major time zones at once, using a ring of city names.
A blade-polishing technique used by Grand Seiko for distortion-free, mirror-like surfaces.
